source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)
revision_note: Newly added with 8 verified chunks under public domain (2026-07-23, Batch 8). Source: Evelyn Underhill's biographical Introduction to Rabindranath Tagore's 1915 translation of Kabir's songs, fetched directly from the sacred-texts.com etext, which states explicitly: 'This text is in the public domain in the US because it was published prior to 1923.' Underhill's introduction itself flags Kabir's traditional biography as 'surrounded by contradictory legends, on none of which reliance can be placed' -- this manifest preserves that framing rather than asserting the legends as verified fact.

content.text: Underhill records that Kabir was 'born in or near Benares, of Mohammedan parents, and probably about the year 1440,' most likely as the son of a Mohammedan weaver of that city. He never adopted the life of the professional ascetic: 'all the legends agree on this point: that Kabir was a weaver, a simple and unlettered man, who earned his living at the loom... he was no ascetic, but a married man, the father of a family... it was from out of the heart of the common life that he sang his rapturous lyrics of divine love.'
content.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

content.text: Tradition holds that the boy Kabir, of Muslim birth, knew a Hindu guru would be unlikely to accept him as a disciple, and so hid on the steps of the Ganges where the celebrated ascetic Ramananda bathed each morning. When Ramananda came down to the water he trod on Kabir's body unexpectedly and exclaimed in astonishment, 'Ram! Ram!' -- the name of his own God. Kabir then declared he had received the mantra of initiation from Ramananda's own lips, and in spite of the protests of orthodox Brahmans and Mohammedans alike, persisted in his claim to discipleship, exhibiting in action the very principle of religious synthesis Ramananda had sought to establish in thought.
content.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

content.text: Kabir denounced empty ritual, whether Hindu or Muslim, as no substitute for direct communion with God: 'The images are all lifeless, they cannot speak: I know, for I have cried aloud to them. The Purana and the Koran are mere words: lifting up the curtain, I have seen.' He taught that God was 'neither in Kaaba nor in Kailash' and that those who sought Him needed not go far, for He was more accessible to 'the washerwoman and the carpenter' than to the self-righteous holy man.
content.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

content.text: Refusing to be claimed by either creed, Kabir said of himself that he was 'at once the child of Allah and of Ram.' He poured contempt on professional sanctity, on the Yogi who 'has a great beard and matted locks, and looks like a goat,' and on all who thought it necessary to flee the world in search of the One Reality who has 'spread His form of love throughout all the world' -- teaching that home and daily life, not the ascetic's cell, were the proper theatre of the soul's love and renunciation.
content.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

content.text: Kabir's rejection of institutional religion made him, in Underhill's words, 'plainly a heretic' in the eyes of both orthodox Hindus and Mohammedans, and he 'was subjected to considerable persecution' with his headquarters in Benares, the very center of priestly influence. He was at least once brought before the Emperor Sikandar Lodi and charged with claiming divine powers after performing a supposed miracle of healing; though his life was spared, he was banished from Benares in the interests of peace around 1495, when he was nearly sixty years of age.
content.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

content.text: Exiled from Benares, Kabir moved among the cities of northern India as the center of a group of disciples, 'continuing in exile that life of apostle and poet of love to which, as he declares in one of his songs, he was destined "from the beginning of time."' In 1518, an old man broken in health, with hands too feeble to make the music he loved, he died at Maghar near Gorakhpur.
content.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

content.text: A legend recorded by Underhill tells that after Kabir's death, his Mohammedan and Hindu disciples disputed over his body -- the Mohammedans wishing to bury it, the Hindus to burn it. As they argued, Kabir himself appeared and told them to lift the shroud and look beneath. They found, in the place of the corpse, a heap of flowers; half were buried by the Mohammedans at Maghar, half carried by the Hindus to Benares to be burned -- 'fitting conclusion to a life which had made fragrant the most beautiful doctrines of two great creeds.'
content.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)
